content: Have you ever wondered how people in ancient times traded silk or spices? If a merchant in ancient India measured a piece of silk using the length of his arm (cubit), and the buyer had longer arms, who do you think got the better deal? The great markets of Mohenjo-Daro faced this exact mystery thousands of years ago!
Why do you think using handspans, footsteps, or arm lengths caused so much confusion in trade and building?

content.title: The Cubit Confusion
content.description: Imagine two people measuring the same table using their handspans. One gets 10 handspans, the other gets 8. The table didn't change size, but their hands are different!

content: To solve this confusion, scientists created a system of Standard Units that is exactly the same for everyone, everywhere. This system is called the International System of Units (SI units). The word 'Meter' comes from the Greek word 'metron', which means 'to measure'.

definition: A standard unit of measurement is a fixed and universally accepted magnitude of a physical quantity, such as a meter for length or a kilogram for mass.

question: Why did people stop using body parts like handspans for measuring lengths?
options: Because body parts are too long
Because the length of body parts varies from person to person
Because they forgot how to count

content: Think about how you buy clothes. If tailors didn't use a standard measuring tape and used their handspans instead, would your uniform fit perfectly? Explain this to a younger sibling next time you visit a tailor.
This connects to mathematics when we learn about geometry, where precise measurements build the foundation for constructing buildings and designing machines.

Measure the length of your study table using your handspan, and then ask an adult to measure it with theirs. Finally, measure it with a ruler in centimeters. Notice the difference and record it in your notebook!
Always remember to keep your eye exactly above the point where you are taking the measurement on a ruler to avoid the parallax error.

Have you ever observed a ceiling fan, a moving car, and a swing in a park? They are all moving, but are they moving in the same way? If we look closely, the world is a giant dance of different motions.
If you throw a ball straight up into the air, and it falls back down, how is its path different from a train moving on a straight track, or the blades of a windmill?

content.title: Paths of Motion
content.description: Visualizing a straight road (rectilinear), a spinning wheel (circular), and a pendulum swinging back and forth (periodic).

content: Motion is simply a change in the position of an object over time. But there are different types! 1. Rectilinear Motion: Moving in a straight line (like a marching parade). 2. Circular Motion: Moving in a circle (like a fan). 3. Periodic Motion: Motion that repeats after a fixed time (like a swing or a pendulum).

definition: Motion along a straight line. The word comes from Latin 'rectus' (straight) and 'linea' (line).

question: Which of the following is an example of periodic motion?
options: A car moving on a straight road
A plucked string of a guitar
A stone falling from a building
An apple rolling on the ground

content: Think about the Earth. It spins like a top (circular motion) and at the same time, it revolves around the Sun every year (periodic motion). Can an object have more than one type of motion at the same time?
Understanding motion is the first step towards Physics! It links directly to learning about speed, velocity, and gravity in higher classes.
Look around your house and find one example each for rectilinear, circular, and periodic motion. Write them down and draw a rough sketch of their path!
Don't confuse periodic motion with circular motion. A fan going around and around is circular, but a pendulum swinging left to right and returning is periodic.
